reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An abnormal direct communication between an artery and a vein that bypasses the capillary bed
May be congenital, acquired through trauma or iatrogenic injury, or surgically created for haemodialysis access
Classic local signs include a palpable thrill and a continuous machinery-like bruit over the lesion
Compression of the fistula can transiently slow the heart rate as venous return and cardiac output fall (Branham or Nicoladoni-Branham sign)
Large or longstanding fistulae shunt blood away from distal tissue and can cause limb ischaemia, venous hypertension, and swelling
High-flow shunting increases venous return and cardiac output and, if substantial, can precipitate high-output cardiac failure
Duplex ultrasound, CT or MR angiography, and catheter angiography characterise the anatomy and haemodynamic impact
Treatment options include observation, endovascular embolisation or stent grafting, and open surgical repair depending on cause, size, and symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: An arteriovenous fistula creates a low-resistance channel that diverts arterial blood directly into the venous system, bypassing the capillary bed. This produces a steal effect that can reduce distal arterial perfusion, while transmission of arterial pressure into the veins causes venous hypertension, dilatation, and secondary tissue changes. The reduced systemic vascular resistance increases venous return, stroke volume, and cardiac output; a large chronic shunt can lead to cardiac chamber enlargement and high-output heart failure. Congenital lesions reflect abnormal vascular development, whereas acquired fistulae follow penetrating trauma, procedures, or erosion between an adjacent artery and vein.
additionalDifferentials: Deep vein thrombosis with limb swelling
Varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound to demonstrate the communication and flow characteristics
CT or MR angiography to map anatomy and feeding and draining vessels
Catheter angiography for detailed assessment and to guide endovascular treatment
Echocardiography to assess cardiac output and chamber size in high-flow lesions
Assessment of distal perfusion and venous hypertension in the affected limb
redFlags: Features of high-output cardiac failure from a large chronic shunt
Distal limb ischaemia from arterial steal threatening tissue viability
Rapid enlargement, haemorrhage, or an expanding pulsatile mass suggesting associated pseudoaneurysm
Severe venous hypertension with skin breakdown or ulceration
reference.prognosis: Small fistulae may remain asymptomatic and be safely observed, while large or high-flow lesions can progressively cause limb complications or cardiac strain and generally require intervention. Outcomes after embolisation or surgical repair are favourable when the lesion is anatomically suitable, though congenital malformations can recur.
pitfalls: Missing an acquired fistula after penetrating trauma or vascular procedures
Overlooking high-output cardiac failure as a consequence of a large chronic shunt
Confusing a fistula with a pseudoaneurysm and choosing the wrong treatment
Underestimating distal ischaemia caused by arterial steal
management: Observation for small, asymptomatic fistulae, which may remain stable
Endovascular embolisation as first-line closure for anatomically suitable lesions
Surgical ligation or repair for fistulae not amenable to endovascular treatment
Ultrasound-guided compression or thrombin injection for iatrogenic femoral access fistulae
Manage high-output cardiac failure with diuretics and neurohormonal therapy while planning definitive closure
Treat limb complications of venous hypertension and distal ischaemia from the steal effect
For dialysis-access fistulae, salvage function while managing steal or aneurysmal degeneration, with duplex and cardiac surveillance of high-flow lesions
